analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for police and other government officials to use excessive force, steal, or destroy evidence.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors and no action since introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create new federal crimes for people acting under government authority, mainly police officers. It would make excessive force a federal offense carrying up to 30 years in prison when someone dies, criminalize officers who steal money or property from people they arrest or search, and make it a federal crime to destroy or interfere with recordings of police activity or to cover up misconduct. Officers who watch excessive force and fail to intervene could also be prosecuted. Cases resulting in death would have no time limit for prosecution; others would have seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed or robbed by police or other officials acting under government authority, including people in jail, prison, or immigration detention, and bystanders who record police activity. Their families would also gain a federal path to criminal accountability when an incident results in death, regardless of how much time has passed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police misconduct and their families

how_it_helps.text: Makes excessive force by officials acting under color of law a federal crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, or up to 30 years when the offense involves an attempt to kill or results in death [S2].

Criminalizes officers who convert to personal use money, property over $25, or controlled substances taken from people in custody or from homes and vehicles they search, with penalties scaling up to 10 years for amounts over $1,000 [S2].

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to 20 years, to destroy recordings of law enforcement activity, use force or arrest threats to stop someone from legally recording police, or otherwise cover up a possible civil-rights violation [S2].
Holds officers who have the duty, opportunity, and ability to stop excessive force but deliberately choose not to liable as if they committed the offense themselves [S2].
Extends the prosecution deadline to seven years for most offenses under the bill and removes it entirely when the offense results in death [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Police officers and other officials acting under government authority, including staff at privately run detention facilities, would face new federal criminal exposure, and federal prosecutors and courts would bear the cost of the added cases. Law enforcement agencies could also face pressure to change training and disciplinary practices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police officers and officials with government authority

drawbacks.text: Critics of federalizing police conduct argue the bill takes cases that are traditionally handled by state prosecutors and turns them into federal crimes, which they say is an inappropriate expansion of federal power over local policing [S2].

The bill's 30-year maximum for excessive force resulting in death and its criminal penalties for failure to intervene would expose officers to severe punishment in situations that often involve split-second decisions, which opponents say could chill legitimate forceful police work; supporters answer that the standard is limited to force the officer knows is excessive or consciously disregards as excessive [S2].
The bill adds to the already large federal criminal code, and new criminal statutes carry costs for prosecutors, defenders, and the prison system that the bill does not fund [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people harmed by police misconduct, the bill closes real gaps: federal civil-rights prosecutions are rare, state prosecutions even rarer, and the existing federal criminal statute for this conduct carries a much shorter one-year prosecution deadline. The costs fall on officers and prosecutors rather than the general public, and the bill builds in protections for legitimate law enforcement purposes, such as taking property as evidence and limiting recording of undercover activity. The strongest fair objection is the risk of over-deterrence in use-of-force decisions, but the bill's knowledge-based standards are designed to reach only clearly excessive force.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 9, 2026 [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action has been taken [S4].
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's position has changed; the bill simply sits in committee. If it stays there, police unions and law enforcement interests are better off, since the new criminal exposure never takes effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement interests, as the bill sits untouched

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create federal criminal penalties for excessive force, theft, and evidence destruction by officials acting under color of law.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred, with no markup or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-controlled Senate Judiciary Committee has not acted on it [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill creates new federal criminal liability for officers who use excessive force, steal property, fail to intervene, or destroy recordings, with prison terms of up to 30 years in death cases. Unions typically oppose expanded individual criminal exposure for officers, while the accountability it creates is the point for victims of misconduct [S2].

The theft provision covers property taken from people in custody at correctional or detention facilities whether run by a government agency or a private entity, so staff at privately run facilities face the same new criminal exposure [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors almost never reach a vote, and this one faces a Republican-controlled committee and Senate. Unless Booker attracts bipartisan cosponsors or attaches it to a larger package, it will likely sit without action until the Congress ends in January 2027.
